title: Find the jars
goal: Learn to write your first lines of code, in the language Julia, and use them to check one report. No coding experience needed, and mistakes are safe here.
story: Toto wrote a report. His boss Itchy wants it checked against the lab notebook. Itchy: "First, practice on a made-up notebook." Momo, who doubts things, will check what you find.
story_more: Itchy's lab keeps springtails, tiny relatives of the snow fleas seen on winter snow, in jars of damp leaf litter. This practice notebook is made up for training: twelve jars in two batches, B04 and B05, on trays T-D, T-E and T-F. Each jar has one row: springtails seen or not seen.
data_label: Practice data, made up for training. Not the case, so nothing here answers the case.

dictionary.means: a name that holds the practice notebook, a table.
the small warm-up table of 4 jars, the same in every lesson.
one column of the table, picked with a dot.
the function length counts the items inside its round brackets.
sum adds a list up; each true counts as 1.
square brackets pick item 7 of a list, by its position.
rows 1 to 6 of the table, a comma, then all columns.

own_work.say: A CSV is a table saved as a file. Put yours beside your code. Install the two packages once. Then change mydata, mydata.csv and site to your own names: the same rule works on your table.
own_work.code:
using Pkg; Pkg.add(["CSV", "DataFrames"])   # first time only
using CSV, DataFrames
mydata = CSV.read("mydata.csv", DataFrame)
mydata[mydata.site .== "A", :]

glossary.means: one instruction you type in the editor, on one line.
the part of the screen on the right where you type.
the button that makes Julia follow your line and show the answer.
the button that puts the starting line back in the editor.
the place marked ___ in a starting line. Type your answer there.
the button that takes you to the next task.
the last task of a round, where you write one line yourself.
a word that holds something, such as logbook. Coders also call it a variable.
a word that does a job on its input, like length or sum.
what a function works on, inside its brackets (R calls it an argument).
the marks ( ) that go after a function's word.
the marks [ ] that make a list or pick part of something.
a mark that opens or closes part of a line: ( ) or [ ].
what a line gives back after you press Run.
several items in a row, in square brackets, such as [4, 7, 1]. Julia also says vector.
one thing in a list.
one piece of information, like 3, true or "B05".
rows and columns of information, like a spreadsheet. Julia calls it a DataFrame.
one line across the table. In logbook, one row is one jar.
one kind of detail running down the table, such as tray_id.
letters and numbers in double quotes, like "B05".
the marks " " that go around text, as in "B05".
two values that mean yes and no. true counts as 1 and false as 0.
yes or no. Julia counts true as 1 and false as 0.
Julia's message when it cannot follow a line. It is safe: nothing breaks, and you can try again.
a place in a list, counted from 1. Position 7 is the seventh item.
picking part of a list or table by its position, with square brackets.
a run of positions written first:last, such as 7:12.
the mark : that makes a range. Alone, it means all columns.
the mark , that separates items, or the rows from the columns.
after a name, takes out one column, as in logbook.batch_id. Before ==, it asks about every item.
a question asked about every row, giving true or false for each.
asks: is it equal to? It gives one true or false.
asks: is it equal to? for every jar, giving one true or false each.
